interest: This file is valuable to historians of the Allied Occupation of Japan, postwar public health, and international religious politics. It highlights the unexpected transnational impact of Japanese social policy, showing how proposed abortion legislation (enacted as the Eugenic Protection Act of 1948) ignited sharp moral outrage among Ceylonese Catholics, who sought to leverage American Christian prestige and the emerging framework of universal human rights to compel SCAP intervention. Concurrently, the file preserves the foundational administrative texts of Japan's 1947–1948 child welfare transformation, documenting how prewar institutionalization and anti-cruelty laws were dismantled in favor of democratic family-centered foster care, maternal health guidance, strict limits on child labor, and Family Court adoption oversight.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
overview: This file (decimal file 894.4055) from the U.S. State Department's central decimal files covers matters of maternal and child welfare, social legislation, and moral customs in occupied Japan during 1948. The file contains two distinct groups of records: diplomatic correspondence from the American Consulate General in Colombo, Ceylon, transmitting a Catholic editorial strongly protesting Japan's proposed legalization of abortion and urging the United States as the occupying power to intervene; and despatches from the Office of the U.S. Political Adviser for Japan in Tokyo forwarding official English translations of key Japanese child welfare legislation. These Japanese records include Cabinet Order No. 11 and Ministry of Welfare Enforcement Regulations for the landmark Child Welfare Law of 1947, as well as Children's Bureau Directive Ji-Hatsu No. 50 ('Functioning of Family Care'), which set forth extensive regulations, standards, and administrative forms for foster home placement, institutional supervision, child labor safeguards, and domestic adoption.

subfiles.about: Transmits a Catholic newspaper article from Colombo protesting proposed Japanese legislation to legalize abortion and requesting U.S. intervention.
subfiles.from: Perry N. Jester, American Consul General, Colombo, Ceylon
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Perry N. Jester forwards to the Secretary of State the text of an article published in the Ceylon Catholic Messenger of April 4, 1948. The article was officially transmitted to the consulate by the Honorary Secretary of the Catholic Writers Movement of Ceylon, who requested that the U.S. government and its representatives in Tokyo be made aware of Catholic concern regarding the proposed legalization of abortion in Japan. Copies of the despatch were also designated for the Political Adviser to SCAP in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 96 from American Consulate General, Colombo, on Catholic Opposition to Abortion in Japan

subfiles.about: Newspaper editorial and commentary from Ceylon condemning proposed Japanese abortion legislation and arguing that the United States as occupying authority bears moral responsibility.
subfiles.summary: The article 'Modern Herods' denounces a Japanese government bill intended to legalize abortion for maternal protection and eugenic prevention of 'inferior' children, equating induced abortion with cold-blooded murder and the slaughter of innocents by Herod. In an accompanying column, 'Parish Gossip: Is America to Blame?', the columnist Chatterbox contends that the bill violates fundamental human rights and warns that the United States, as the occupying tutor of Japan, will be held accountable before world opinion and divine justice if it fails to prevent this legislation. The author appeals to America's Christian heritage and moral leadership to halt the statutory approval of the measure.
subfiles.title: Clipping from Ceylon Catholic Messenger: 'Modern Herods' and 'Is America to Blame?'
subfiles.to: General Public and U.S. Government / SCAP

subfiles.about: Transmits approved English translations of Japanese cabinet orders and regulations executing the Child Welfare Law.
subfiles.from: W. H. Lawrence, Jr., Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser for Japan transmits five copies each of approved translations of the Cabinet Order for Enforcement of Child Welfare Law and the Enforcement Regulation of Child Welfare Law to the Secretary of State. The despatch notes that the order and regulation became effective on January 1, 1948, except for provisions relating to Article 63, which came into effect on April 1, 1948.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 258 from Acting Political Adviser, Tokyo, Transmitting Child Welfare Regulations

subfiles.about: Ministerial ordinance setting detailed operational rules for Child Welfare Centers, health guidance, maternal handbooks, foster placement, and nursery teacher testing.
subfiles.summary: Promulgated as Kosei Shorei No. 11, this ministerial ordinance establishes comprehensive administrative regulations under the Child Welfare Law. It defines the establishment, jurisdiction, and supervisory functions of Child Welfare Centers; health guidance procedures; and rules for issuing, using, and returning Maternal-and-Child Handbooks (including access to special rations). The regulations also establish procedures for institutional admission, foster home registries, examination standards and subjects for nursery teachers, expense reimbursements, and the repeal of prewar child welfare and anti-cruelty ordinances.
subfiles.title: Enforcement Regulation of Child Welfare Law (Ministry of Welfare Ordinance No. 11)

subfiles.about: Cabinet order governing the composition of child welfare boards, personnel qualifications, juvenile institutions, and public subsidy allocations.
subfiles.summary: This Cabinet Order details the administrative apparatus required to implement the Child Welfare Law, defining the membership, tenure, quorum, and officer appointments for Central and Local Child Welfare Boards. It sets professional and educational qualifications for Child Welfare Officials and nursery teachers, mandates prefectural and national Kyogo-in reform facilities, and authorizes placing indigent mothers and children in private welfare agencies. It also defines formulas, accounting methods, and penalty recovery clauses for national and prefectural welfare subsidies.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Order for Enforcement of Child Welfare Law

subfiles.about: Administrative directive and standardized forms establishing comprehensive procedures for foster care, child labor regulation, and legal adoption.
subfiles.from: Children's Bureau, Ministry of Welfare, Japan
subfiles.summary: Issued as directive Ji-Hatsu No. 50, this document sets forth detailed instructions and philosophy for promoting family foster care and legal adoption over institutionalization for dependent, neglected, and orphaned children. It prescribes strict criteria for investigating prospective foster homes, supervising child nutrition, schooling, and health, and regulating work under the Labor Standards Law, strictly forbidding child exploitation and hazardous labor. The directive also details adoption procedures coordinated through Child Welfare Centers and the Court of Domestic Relations (Family Court), and provides five official application and investigation forms (Forms No. 1 through No. V).
subfiles.title: Children's Bureau Directive Ji-Hatsu No. 50: 'Functioning of Family Care'
subfiles.to: Prefectural Governors and Child Welfare Centers
